newsitem.title: USA: U.S.Senate panel delays work on encryption exports.
newsitem.headline: U.S.Senate panel delays work on encryption exports.

text.p: The Senate Commerce Committee canceled a Thursday drafting session on a bill to ease export controls on computer encoding technology after one Senator objected.

In a letter to Committee Chairman Sen. Larry Pressler, Sen. James Exon said he opposed the mark-up of the Promotion of Commerce Online in the Digital Era Act of 1996, known as Pro-CODE. He cited unresolved national security and law enforcment concerns.

The bill is opposed by the Clinton administration but has bipartisan support. It could be marked up later in the month, but time is running short in the current congressional session, according to a staffer for Sen. Conrad Burns, one of the bill's primary sponsors.
"We still hope to get something out this session," the staffer said.

Burns said earlier in the week that he did not expect the bill to become law this session. But he said he hoped the Commerce Committee would approve it to send a message to the bill's opponents and set the stage for passage next year.
Some staffers and lobbyists speculated the drafting session was done in by rumors that the Clinton administration was about to come forward with a new compromise proposal.
But a spokeswoman in Vice President Al Gore's office said late Wednesday that no new compromise was expected.

Rather, the administration plans to formally release soon a plan Gore announced in July that would ease export restrictions only if encryption users agree to keep duplicate software keys in escrow and accessible to the government with proper authority, the spokeswoman said.
The plan is also expected to recommend transfering jurisdiction over encryption export licensing from the State Department to the Commerce Department.
